query: I am interested in high-entropy alloys for extreme temperature applications. How can we predict melting properties such as the melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity for multi-component systems where experimental data is sparse or unreliable due to high melting points? I am looking for a hypothesis on a computational methodology that balances accuracy with the need to screen vast compositional spaces, along with prior evidence on why standard approaches struggle in this regime and what a valid boundary condition for such a method would be.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid computational framework integrating CALPHAD thermodynamic modeling with machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on first-principles data can accurately predict melting temperatures, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity for refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) in compositional spaces where experimental data is sparse, provided the system remains within the single-phase solid solution regime.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-principal-element alloy system (≥5 elements) composed primarily of refractory metals (e.g., Nb, Mo, Ta, W, V) with a body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution structure, potentially containing minor additions of Al, Ti, or Si to tune phase stability.
generation.intervention: Construct a hybrid computational workflow: (1) Use CALPHAD to rapidly screen phase stability and identify single-phase regions to avoid complex multiphase thermodynamic calculations; (2) Generate a training dataset of structural and thermodynamic properties using first-principles KKR-CPA or DFT calculations for representative compositions; (3) Train a machine-learned interatomic potential (e.g., EAM or Lennard-Jones variants) on this dataset; (4) Perform molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using the trained potential to calculate melting points (via heating/cooling cycles), entropy of fusion, and heat capacity.
generation.conditions: The method is applied to refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) operating in the temperature range of 1000 K to 2500 K, where experimental measurement is difficult due to extreme melting points and reactivity. The system must be within the single-phase solid solution regime to ensure the validity of the thermodynamic models used in the screening phase.
generation.structural_mediator: Severe local lattice distortion caused by the size mismatch of multiple principal elements, which impedes dislocation motion and alters vibrational entropy, thereby influencing the melting behavior and heat capacity.
generation.mechanism: Standard approaches struggle because classical force fields lack transferability across the vast compositional space of HEAs, and first-principles calculations are computationally prohibitive for screening large compositional spaces. The proposed hybrid method overcomes this by using CALPHAD to restrict the search to thermodynamically stable single-phase regions (reducing the combinatorial space) and using machine-learned potentials to capture the complex local atomic environments and anharmonic vibrational effects critical for accurate melting predictions at a fraction of the cost of full first-principles MD.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid framework will yield melting temperature predictions with an error margin of <5% compared to available experimental data for known RHEAs (e.g., NbMoTaW, NbMoTaWV) and will successfully predict the trend of melting point depression or elevation upon minor alloying additions (e.g., V or Ti) that are difficult to measure experimentally. It will also provide accurate estimates of the entropy of fusion derived from the latent heat and melting temperature in the MD simulations.
generation.baseline: Traditional CALPHAD methods alone, which often rely on extrapolated thermodynamic databases that may be inaccurate for complex multi-component systems, or pure first-principles molecular dynamics, which is too computationally expensive to screen vast compositional spaces.
generation.boundary: The method is valid only for systems that form single-phase solid solutions (BCC or FCC) as predicted by CALPHAD. It may fail for systems prone to significant phase separation, intermetallic precipitation, or amorphization, as the training data for the potential would not capture the complex multiphase thermodynamics required for accurate melting prediction in those regimes. Additionally, the method assumes the validity of the classical potential form for the specific refractory elements involved.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the transferability of the machine-learned potential to compositions significantly outside the training set, particularly if the local coordination environments change drastically. Furthermore, the accuracy of the CALPHAD screening depends on the quality of the underlying thermodynamic databases for refractory systems, which may be incomplete or unreliable for certain high-order combinations.

falsification_experiment.design: Select three refractory HEA compositions (e.g., NbMoTaW, NbMoTaWV, and a novel quinary variant) that have been experimentally synthesized and for which melting temperatures have been measured via high-temperature calorimetry or optical pyrometry. Run the proposed hybrid workflow (CALPHAD screening + ML-potential MD) to predict their melting temperatures. Compare the predicted values against the experimental measurements.
measurements: Predicted melting temperature (Tm_pred) from MD simulations
Entropy of fusion (ΔS_f) derived from simulation latent heat
Heat capacity (Cp) vs. Temperature curves from simulation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the predicted melting temperatures for any of the three test cases deviate from the experimental values by more than 10%, or if the predicted entropy of fusion deviates by more than 15%, indicating that the hybrid approach cannot accurately capture the thermodynamics of these extreme temperature systems.

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. “Superalloy” is the general name given to iron-based, nickel-based, and cobalt-based alloys, given their high endurance, creep, and fatigue strength at high temperature. They are widely used in aviation, aerospace, and automotive and chemical industries, serving in high-temperature (≤ 1100 °C) environments. However, for super high temperature conditions of up to 1500 °C and 3000 °C, traditional surperalloys are powerless. Instead, a new type of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown their advantages. High-entropy alloys or multi-element alloys are loosely defined as solid-solution alloys that contain more than five principal elements in equal or near equal atomic percent (at%) [ [1] , [2] , [3] ]. HEAs usually have unexpected properties, such as high strength, high hardness, excellent softening resistance, and wear and corrosion resistance [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. According to the cocktail effects of HEAs, the alloy properties can be adjusted by composition changes and via alloying [ [4] , [5] , [10] ]. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
